chunks: "On a PCB, ground is two things at once.
It's the reference node, the zero volts everything is measured against, and it's the return path, the route every bit of current takes to get back to its source.
The schematic draws it as one symbol, but on the board it's real copper, and real copper has resistance and inductance. That's why it matters.
When current flows through a ground conductor, it creates a voltage drop, I times R at low frequency and L di/dt at high frequency.
If two circuits share that conductor, one circuit's current moves the other circuit's zero.

So a digital block switching a hundred milliamps in a couple of nanoseconds through ten nanohenries of ground trace lifts the local ground by half a volt, and a nearby sensor or ADC reads it as signal.
The same thing at the level of loops: the return current's loop area sets how much it radiates and picks up.

The fix is mostly to give the return currents a low impedance, well-defined path: a solid ground plane directly under the signals, short connections to it with vias at every ground pin, and care about where large currents flow so they don't pass through sensitive references.
That makes grounding the biggest factor in noise, signal integrity and EMI."
